title: Induction-hardened medium-carbon bar instead of a through-hardened alloy bar

ideaData.title: Induction-hardened medium-carbon bar instead of a through-hardened alloy bar
ideaData.technicalDescription: How it works (benchmark as named by the study): The bar is loaded in torsion at the spline runs, not along its whole length. Induction hardening puts the hardness where the load is. This is normal practice; the aftermarket's 4340 chromoly shafts exist for modified vehicles on oversize tyres, which is a different duty from ours. SPEC: bar grade C50 / 1050 induction-hardened on the spline runs, case depth 1.5-2.5 mm* on the flanks, shot peened; torsional capability held at the 15,539 Nm* design case
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Cost effect (study): -£1.56*. SPEC: bar grade C50 / 1050 induction-hardened on the spline runs, case depth 1.5-2.5 mm* on the flanks, shot peened; torsional capability held at the 15,539 Nm* design case
ideaData.riskNotes: Duty / environment: Re-validate. Torsional fatigue rig at the design case, and confirm the spline runout is inside the hardened zone. Trade-off: Proven · effort Low. Trade: no headroom for a future torque increase without revisiting the bar.
ideaData.powertrain: ICE / MHEV (longitudinal I6 ~500 Nm, V8 ~700 Nm, 8AT — study reference vehicle)
ideaData.targetVehicle: SCOPE: front pair and rear pair of constant-velocity half-shafts for the reference vehicle in A1 (longitudinal I6 ~500 Nm, V8 ~700 Nm, 8AT rated 750 Nm INPUT, transfer case low range 2.93:1, final drive 3.54, 33-in tyres at 0.40 m rolling radius, 3,300 kg GVW, 3,500 kg braked tow, 900 mm wading, 240,000 km, EU plant, >=80,000/yr, 2026 prices). ARCHITECTURE ASSUMPTION, stated loudly: independent front AND rear suspension, so four CV half-shafts. If the rear goes to a solid axle this line largely disappears — see idea D1. DIRECTIONAL should-cost, not a validated teardown BOM. Every rate below is an input you can argue with.
ideaData.studyCombinedCapture: COMBINED CAPTURE — honest, and NOT the sum. The saving cards add to roughly £141 and that number is wrong for four reasons. D1 is £104 of it and it is an architecture decision that belongs to the programme director, not to a cost workshop. D2 is very likely infeasible on a longitudinal SUV and a rejected idea captures nothing. D5 is ruled out by published plunge travel unless a long-plunge variant exists, so it is not a saving at all — it is an adder that is currently unavailable. And P1, P2, P3 and P4 are all things the SUPPLIER does, so we capture them through the RFQ rather than in our own plant. A realistic engineering-only capture, excluding D1 and D2, is £29-38* gross; net of the M4 and D4 adders it is £17-26* on a £423 assembly, roughly 4-6%. Add the RFQ at -12% and it becomes £69-78*. THAT is the number to commit to, and it says the same thing the transfer-case study said: the commercial lever beats the engineering levers, and we should pull it first.

title: Keep TPE on the outer front boot — refuse the chloroprene saving

title: Keep two different greases and a stated temperature capability — refuse the single-grease saving

ideaData.title: Keep two different greases and a stated temperature capability — refuse the single-grease saving
ideaData.technicalDescription: How it works (benchmark as named by the study): The fixed joint wants a high-pressure moly charge; the plunging joint wants a low-friction charge that keeps generated axial force down. Moly disulfide films break down past roughly 180 C, and sustained low-range crawl is a heat case with no airflow. SPEC: fixed-joint grease rated above 180 C*; plunging-joint grease specified to hold measured GAF under 1,500 N* at 3,000 Nm; fill quantity to plus or minus 2%*
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Cost effect (study): £0 — a £0.69* saving refused. SPEC: fixed-joint grease rated above 180 C*; plunging-joint grease specified to hold measured GAF under 1,500 N* at 3,000 Nm; fill quantity to plus or minus 2%*
ideaData.riskNotes: Duty / environment: PROTECTED LINE. This is the sustained-crawl duty case, which is the vehicle's headline capability. Trade-off: Proven · effort Low. Trade: two part numbers and two dispensers instead of one.

title: Specify steel cleanliness on the joint races

title: Hard-turn the rear outer joint ball tracks instead of grinding them

ideaData.title: Hard-turn the rear outer joint ball tracks instead of grinding them

ideaData.targetVehicle: SCOPE: front pair and rear pair of constant-velocity half-shafts for the reference vehicle in A1 (longitudinal I6 ~500 Nm, V8 ~700 Nm, 8AT rated 750 Nm INPUT, transfer case low range 2.93:1, final drive 3.54, 33-in tyres at 0.40 m rolling radius, 3,300 kg GVW, 3,500 kg braked tow, 900 mm wading, 240,000 km, EU plant, >=80,000/yr, 2026 prices). ARCHITECTURE ASSUMPTION, stated loudly: independent front AND rear suspension, so four CV half-shafts. If the rear goes to a solid axle this line largely disappears — see idea D1. DIRECTIONAL should-cost, not a validated teardown BOM. Every rate below is an input you can argue with.
ideaData.studyCombinedCapture: COMBINED CAPTURE — honest, and NOT the sum. The saving cards add to roughly £141 and that number is wrong for four reasons. D1 is £104 of it and it is an architecture decision that belongs to the programme director, not to a cost workshop. D2 is very likely infeasible on a longitudinal SUV and a rejected idea captures nothing. D5 is ruled out by published plunge travel unless a long-plunge variant exists, so it is not a saving at all — it is an adder that is currently unavailable. And P1, P2, P3 and P4 are all things the SUPPLIER does, so we capture them through the RFQ rather than in our own plant. A realistic engineering-only capture, excluding D1 and D2, is £29-38* gross; net of the M4 and D4 adders it is £17-26* on a £423 assembly, roughly 4-6%. Add the RFQ at -12% and it becomes £69-78*. THAT is the number to commit to, and it says the same thing the transfer-case study said: the commercial lever beats the engineering levers, and we should pull it first.
